record.paper_title: Similarity: generalizations, applications and open problems
record.original_question: Can modern symmetry approaches be developed into systematic symmetry-based techniques for identifying candidate intermediate-asymptotic solutions of partial differential equations, in the setting where similarity solutions are used to describe intermediate-asymptotic behavior for wide classes of PDEs?

artifact.status_search_result: The question is a programmatic research direction rather than a single precise conjecture. Available references (Barenblatt's monograph on scaling and intermediate asymptotics, Olver's and Bluman's work on symmetry methods, and surveys of nonclassical/potential symmetries) develop partial machinery — Lie-group reductions, nonclassical symmetries, and renormalization-group approaches — that yields first-kind and, in some cases, second-kind similarity solutions, but no systematic, fully general algorithm guaranteeing identification of all intermediate-asymptotic candidates for broad PDE classes has been established. The status is therefore best regarded as open with substantial partial progress.

status_evidence.title: Scaling, Self-similarity, and Intermediate Asymptotics
status_evidence.snippet: Barenblatt's framework distinguishes first-kind (dimensional) and second-kind (anomalous) self-similar solutions describing intermediate asymptotics.
status_evidence.claim: Existing theory provides conceptual framework but not a fully systematic symmetry-based algorithm.

status_evidence.title: Symmetry Methods for Differential Equations
status_evidence.snippet: Lie symmetry techniques yield similarity reductions for PDEs.
status_evidence.claim: Modern symmetry methods supply partial machinery but do not constitute a complete systematic procedure for intermediate asymptotics.

status_evidence.title: Symmetry and Explicit Solutions of Partial Differential Equations (Olver)
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses classical, nonclassical, and generalized symmetry approaches to explicit and similarity solutions.
status_evidence.claim: Generalized symmetry approaches remain an active area; no general algorithm for intermediate-asymptotic candidate detection is established.

A self-similar (or similarity) solution of a partial differential equation is a solution that is invariant under a one-parameter group of scaling transformations of the independent and dependent variables, so that, via a similarity variable combining the independent variables, the PDE is reduced to a problem in fewer independent variables. Such solutions frequently describe the intermediate-asymptotic behavior of solutions to wide classes of PDEs: namely, the behavior in regimes where the influence of fine details of initial and/or boundary data has been forgotten but the system has not yet reached its ultimate (e.g. equilibrium) state. Classical similarity solutions of the first kind have scaling exponents fixed by dimensional analysis; second-kind similarity solutions have exponents determined by nonlinear eigenvalue problems and are typically not detectable by dimensional analysis alone. Modern symmetry methods for differential equations include Lie point symmetries, contact and higher (generalized) symmetries, nonclassical and conditional symmetries, potential and nonlocal symmetries, equivalence transformations, and related group-theoretic constructions.

Problem. Develop modern symmetry approaches into a systematic, algorithmic family of symmetry-based techniques whose output, applied to a given partial differential equation (or class of PDEs) together with auxiliary conditions, is a list of candidate intermediate-asymptotic solutions describing the long-time, short-time, or far-field behavior of broad classes of solutions. More precisely, construct procedures that:

(i) take as input a PDE (or system) together with a specified asymptotic regime of interest;
(ii) produce, in finitely many constructive steps using symmetry-group machinery (Lie, generalized, nonclassical, potential, equivalence, etc.), a finite list of candidate self-similar or asymptotic ansätze, including those of the second kind with anomalous scaling exponents;
(iii) come with verifiable criteria guaranteeing that each candidate so produced actually captures the intermediate-asymptotic behavior of an identifiable class of initial/boundary value problems for the given PDE.
